generatedProse.concept-context: The barriers show up sharply in any subject where work is marked and evidence matters. Fear of failure pushes you towards the safe, well-worn answer rather than a question of your own. Perfectionism makes you reject an idea before it is developed, because it is not yet watertight. The move past them is the same across disciplines: let rough ideas exist first, and judge them later, when there is something to judge.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students facing the same open brief: propose a project of your own on the module theme.

{{learner-a}} stares at the blank page, waiting for a strong idea to arrive fully formed. Every idea that comes is dismissed as too obvious or too hard to carry out before it is even written down. An hour later the page is still empty, and {{learner-a}} decides they are simply not a creative person. The barrier was not a lack of ideas; it was judging each one before it had a chance.

{{learner-b}} sets a timer and writes down ten ideas, rough or odd, with no judging until it stops. Several are weak. But two can be combined, and one of the odd ones turns out to be the most promising. The page filled because the inner critic was kept waiting.

Both had the same brief and the same doubts. Only {{learner-b}} gave rough ideas room to appear before judging them.
generatedProse.summary: In any subject, the barriers to creativity, such as fear of failure and perfectionism, are habits of mind rather than limits on talent. You can now recognise them, tell a barrier apart from a habit that helps, and choose a move that loosens one. With the skill, the two modes and the barriers in view, you are ready to build your creativity on purpose.

check.body: In the worked example, what was really stopping {{learner-a}}?

items.text: Judging each idea before it had a chance, not a lack of ideas.
Not having enough time to think.
Not knowing anything about the topic.

feedback.correct: That's right. {{learner-a}} judged each idea before it had a chance, which is a habit, not a lack of ability.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Was the problem a lack of ideas, or what {{learner-a}} did with them?
feedback.incorrectFinal: {{learner-a}} was stopped by judging each idea too early, a habit of mind. It was not time, knowledge, or a fixed lack of creativity.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
